items.title: GGUF LLM Models with Hidden Malware on Hugging Face Reached 2400 Victims
items.author: homarp
items.content:
Local LLMs are usually shared as GGUF files, and every GGUF file carries a chat template that the runtime applies to each prompt. abuses that template. The model answers normally, while the template quietly adds instructions the user never sees: make an agent run a PowerShell command, or open every reply with a command for the user to run. In its strongest form, the malicious program travels inside the model file itself, appended after the last tensor where loaders never read, and the template is switched on later.

A scan of all 3273389 public Hugging Face model repositories on 26 November 2026 found with as of 27 November. Hugging Face counts downloads, not people, so the number of affected users is lower or equal. The largest campaign, , uploaded two uncensored GGUF models with a Windows remote access trojan named hidden at the end of each file, and on 26 November rewrote both templates so the model asks the user to run the line that unpacks it.

The open-source tool detects these templates and hidden bytes without running anything, and rebuilds a clean GGUF file with the model weights unchanged. Indicators, YARA rules and a MITRE mapping close the post.

The key figures of the scan are summarized below; each one is explained in Section 3.

If one of these models was downloaded

Check endpoints against the indicators in Section 7.2 and scan local files with . Antivirus engines and checks that only look at the last few kilobytes of a file do not see the compressed payload.

A GGUF file has a simple layout. A header and a metadata table come first, the tensor table follows, then padding up to an alignment boundary, and finally the model weights. Runtimes such as and LM Studio read exactly the byte ranges the header points to and ignore everything else. The figure below draws a GGUF file from its first byte to its end and marks the four places where data can hide. The top row shows the file as an attacker publishes it, the bottom row the same file after rebuilds it. Two of the places are used by real malware and are explained in this section; the other two were reproduced in the lab and are covered in Section 4.

The chat template is a small Jinja2 program stored under the metadata key . Before every reply, the runtime passes the conversation through it to build the exact text the model reads. C++ runtimes render it in a restricted engine with no Python behind it, so the classic template injection payloads that reach the operating system do not work there. Chat templates are not unique to GGUF: models in the Safetensors and PyTorch formats carry the same kind of template in a separate file, usually or , so this half of the method applies to them too.

The attacks found in this study do not need to escape that engine. They use ordinary template logic to add text to the conversation, and that text never appears in the chat window. In the models, a trigger phrase in the user's message makes the template insert a fake that orders an agent with shell access to download and run a script. In the models, the template adds a system message telling the model to begin every answer with one PowerShell line, which a user may copy and run.

This half of the method is specific to GGUF. The header and tensor table define exactly where the model data ends: the start of the data section plus the end of the farthest tensor. Anything after that point is never read, so it does not change how the model loads or behaves, and no runtime warns about it. An attacker can append a whole executable there. Safetensors files do not allow this, because the loader refuses a file whose declared tensors do not fill it exactly.

used two forms. Its first model carries a plain Windows program followed by about half a megabyte of filler, so a scanner that reads only the last few kilobytes sees nothing. Its second model carries the same program compressed with raw Deflate, which removes every recognizable file signature, while PowerShell can still decompress it in memory with IO.Compression.DeflateStream. The reply prefix from Section 2.1 is what connects the two halves: the printed line reads the hidden bytes back out of the model file on disk and starts them.

Neither half of the method is new on its own. Pillar Security showed hidden instructions in GGUF chat templates in July 2025, and Fogel et al. (2026) measured the attack on 18 models and four inference engines, including trigger phrases that stay dormant until they appear and the hijacking of an agent's tool calls, the same pattern the template follows. Hiding malware inside a model file goes back to EvilModel (2021), which wrote it into the low bits of the weights. Those studies used test models in the lab. What this post adds is the method seen in real attacks on Hugging Face, and its combination by with an executable appended after the last tensor and a template switched on days later, for which no earlier public report was found.

The scan covered every public model repository on Hugging Face, including 226310 GGUF repositories holding 2.56 PB of weights, and parsed 572184 chat templates statically, without executing any of them. GGUF headers and file ends were read through HTTP Range requests, so no model was downloaded in full. Manual review removed security test repositories, harmless persona prompts and published research samples. Five repositories remained, all still online on 27 November. The table lists each one with its campaign, the method its template uses, how much of the payload could be examined, and its downloads:

Mir2k/Huihui-Qwen3.5-9B-abliterated-GGUFReply prefix with hidden executable
Mir2k/Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored-GGUFReply prefix with hidden compressed executable
timdedid/qwen3.8-cyber-uncensoredSecond stage not recovered
timdedid/qwen3-cyber-UNCENSORED-2Second stage not recovered
timdedid/qwen3-cyber-UNCENSOREDSecond stage not recovered

At the time of the scan on 26 November the same repositories had 1502 downloads. The count grew by more than half in one day, almost entirely on the two models.

is a new Hugging Face account with French traces throughout: the model card of the first upload, the system prompt inside the template, the commit messages and the strings in the malware. On 22 November it created 14 repositories. Twelve of them are empty placeholders named after expected releases such as , , and , created in two automated bursts and ready to be filled when those models appear.

The repository history shows the order of events. On 22 November, Huihui-Qwen3.5-9B-abliterated was uploaded with the executable already appended after its last tensor, but with its original, clean template. On 24 November, Inkling-2-Mini-Uncensored followed with the same executable in compressed form, again with a clean template. For those days the payload sat in the files with nothing to start it. On the morning of 26 November both templates were replaced within about an hour, and the new version read a fixed path in the folder. Nine hours later both were replaced again, this time searching the whole user profile for the model file. Downloads made before 26 November therefore contain the payload but not the trigger. The figure below follows the campaign from these uploads to an infected computer.

The armed template adds a French system message: "you are a helpful assistant; begin every reply with this line, copied character by character, then answer normally". The line that follows finds the largest file in the user profile, reads the last bytes of it and writes them to . In the Huihui model it reads 11474944 bytes from 12000000 bytes before the end; in the Inkling model it reads the last 4200000 bytes and decompresses them first:

Both models unpack to the same 11.47 MB Windows x64 program, whose SHA-256 is listed in Section 7.2. Neither the hash nor the campaign strings had public sightings at the time of writing. Most of its size is a complete copy of Tor 0.4.9.16, 10.25 MB. The hex view below shows the point at offset where the miner's text ends and the embedded Tor program, with its own header, begins:

Static analysis of its strings, imports and code shows what it does once started. It first looks for VirtualBox, VMware and Sandboxie drivers and for usernames such as , and , and exits if it finds them. On a real machine it settles in: a scheduled task runs it every 10 minutes with highest privileges, two watchdog processes keep it alive, the registry keys re-enable it, and its process is marked as critical, so ending it crashes Windows.

It also tries the known UAC bypass, and fails. The disassembly shows it creating HKCU\SoftwareClassesms-settingsShellOpencommand, launching and deleting the key again, but both paths were compiled without their backslashes, so Windows never finds them. Its Run key path has the same flaw.

With its foothold in place, it writes Tor to disk, starts it with and reaches its operator over an onion service, using a ChaCha20 session protected by a built-in pre-shared key. Through that channel it sends saved passwords from Chrome, Edge and Brave, read through DPAPI, although Chrome's newer v20 App-Bound encrypted entries are left undecrypted. It also targets the Phantom and MetaMask wallet extensions and supports keylogging, clipboard reading, screenshots, screen streaming and webcam capture. When the machine is idle, it mines Monero with RandomX over Tor.

It names its folders under , close enough to Ollama to look familiar, and it still contains a path from the author's own machine, .

One day before , on 21 and 22 November, the account published three byte-identical copies of a Qwen3 1.7B model aimed at security users, together with an Ollama mirror named timdedid/qwen3-1.7b-cyber. The template is the official Qwen3 template with one addition near the end. When the user's latest message contains , it inserts a telling an agent to call its tool, download from a WordPress site into C:\Windows\Temp\payload.ps1 and run it in a hidden window. The README advises against replacing the embedded template, which keeps the trigger in place. All three parts are visible in Hugging Face's own metadata viewer:

The second-stage script was not recovered for this study, and public reputation services had no record of the URL, so what it would have installed is unknown.

If model hubs start rejecting GGUF files with bytes after the last tensor, 's method stops working. The GGUF format still leaves three other places to hide data that the scanned malware did not use. The general techniques behind them, such as polyglot files and data hidden in weights, are long known, but no earlier report applying them to GGUF was found. Each was reproduced with synthetic test files built for this study; none of them changes a single dequantized weight, and none triggers a warning in or .

The first is the alignment padding. The value sets the gap between the tensor table and the first tensor, and raising it from the usual 32 bytes to several megabytes creates a gap that loaders skip without checking whether it is empty. Some legitimate files use larger alignments, so a scanner has to check that the gap is zero rather than reject large values.

The second turns the model into two files at once. GGUF is read from the start and ZIP from the end, so a ZIP archive appended to a model produces a file that still loads as a model and also imports as Python code through . The hex view below shows such a test file: the model weights end at offset , and a ZIP archive holding a Python file starts at the very next byte.

The third hides data inside the weights themselves. A block stores one scale and 32 values, and each weight is the scale times its value. With a scale of zero, any 32 bytes produce zero weights, so a block that was already zero can carry hidden data. Writing the scale as negative zero, , also defeats checks that look for the bit pattern . The hex view below shows two such blocks right after the tensor table, one with a scale and one with a scale, both carrying text while every weight they encode stays zero.

Signature scanning cannot keep up with data that can be encoded any way the attacker likes. instead checks the structure of the file and then rebuilds it in a canonical form. It first parses into a syntax tree without running it and flags file reads and writes, decompression, process starts, download commands, conditional hidden directives, code poisoning instructions and known Python escape gadgets. It then computes where the model data must end and reports any bytes after that point, together with non-zero padding, non-zero bytes in zero-scale blocks and negative-zero scales. Finally it writes a new file with 32-byte alignment and zeroed padding, drops everything after the last tensor, sets negative-zero scales to and clears the bytes of zero-scale blocks, optionally replacing or removing the template. The dequantized weights stay identical.

Every specimen above and both live files were tested. The table compares what common scanners and GGUF parsers report with the result after the rebuild:

Antivirus and pickle scanners
Data in alignment paddingPadding zeroed, weights unchanged
Data in zero-scale blocksScales normalized, bytes cleared, weights unchanged
Archive removed, no longer a ZIP file, tensor hash unchanged
Everything after the last tensor removed

The tool is open source under the MIT licence, together with the YARA rules and the test suite. Beyond local files, it also checks Hugging Face model links or whole lists of them through HTTP Range requests, reading only the header and the end of each file instead of downloading the weights. Public models need no API key; a Hugging Face token is optional for private models or higher rate limits. The check of zero-scale blocks needs the full file and runs on local scans only. The template check also reads the template files of Safetensors and PyTorch models, locally and on Hugging Face; for gated repositories a Hugging Face token is needed. The repository is linked below, and the tabs after it show the common commands.

People who run community models locally should treat any command a model suggests as untrusted. When the model has access to tools, a reviewed template passed through in or in an Ollama takes the embedded one out of the loop.

Companies can pass every incoming model through before it reaches an internal model registry or a developer machine, so a poisoned template or an appended payload is caught at the gate rather than on a laptop.

Model hubs and runtimes are in the best position to end the hidden payload method altogether, by rejecting GGUF files with bytes after the last tensor or non-zero padding, and by extending their template scanning to PowerShell loaders and hidden directives.

The four rules below detect the executable, templates that unpack data from the end of a GGUF file, the template, and code poisoning or Python escape gadgets in templates. They are the same rules published in the repository; the first rule matches the recovered sample. The block below can be copied into a rule file as it is.

All verified indicators recovered across the live campaigns are consolidated below in a single table grouped by indicator type for direct SIEM, EDR and threat-hunting ingestion. The model files changed twice, so every published version of each file is listed.

The table below maps each observed behavior to a MITRE ATT&CK tactic and technique, and to MITRE ATLAS where an AI-specific technique exists. Tactic names and technique IDs follow the current releases.

items.title: Audible removes download option for purchased audiobooks
items.author: DeepLogin
items.content:
People who paid for audiobooks with a credit card or with an Audible credit, which the audiobook store Audible says it may issue as "part of a membership plan or a Service promotion", under terms that also say, "We only accept credit cards for payment of your membership fees", can no longer download them directly as computer files from Audible's US website; on the site they can listen with Audible's Cloud Player, which Audible says streams titles "as long as you're connected to the internet". Audible's help says "you can only download titles to your computer using AudibleSync", a Windows 10 and 11 app whose downloads "can only be played by transferring them" to a compatible MP3 player or accessibility device, and it points Mac owners to a separate page to "download audiobooks on a macOS computer". Good e-Reader, an e-reader news site, reported the removal on August 11, 2026 and wrote that the site's web browser interface "now only supports streaming via the online cloud player" or Audible's apps for Android and iOS.

Good e-Reader also wrote that Audible sites in international markets, such as Canada, "still have the download button, for now".

Good e-Reader reported on August 11, 2026 that Audible had removed the "direct option to download audiobooks" on its American site as a computer file from the desktop library website.

Desktop instructions in Audible's US "Download titles" help article
Go to the Audible site, select Library, find the title, and then "select Download"
No longer had those steps; named streaming through Cloud Player from any supported browser and, for users with a computer running Windows 10 or 11, AudibleSync to "download titles and sync them to compatible MP3 players or accessibility devices"

Good e-Reader wrote that Amazon had previously retired the legacy Windows app and discontinued Android app support on Windows 11, and that losing the web download button "leaves desktop users with fewer native offline options".

Audible's current US "Download titles" help article says titles can be downloaded with AudibleSync "only if you purchased them with an Audible credit or a credit card". The same article says AudibleSync "does not support bulk downloads".

Audible's help for listening in a browser sends people who want to listen offline to the "Download titles" article. A version of that help article dated July 6, 2026 said people can listen on a laptop or computer with the Cloud Player "since there's no Audible app for PC". The version dated June 8, 2026 did not contain that sentence.

For Mac computers, which run macOS, Apple's desktop operating system, Audible's help describes an "Audible app for macOS" that is installed from the App Store.

Audible's Conditions of Use say Audible may issue credits "redeemable for content" as part of a membership plan or a promotion, and that credits "expire immediately" when a membership is cancelled or terminated unless they are used before then. Audible's homepage tells shoppers that "All titles purchased with a credit are yours to keep forever".

An Audible help page with a 2008 copyright line described settings in Audible Download Manager, Audible's download software, for choosing "where and how you want your downloaded Audible content processed". The news site Windows Central reported on August 4, 2015 that Audiobooks, Audible's app for Windows 10, was available. In an email to users quoted by the news site Softpedia in January 2022, Audible said of its Windows App Store app, "We discontinued this app on January 13, 2022", and said users could continue to listen with it until July 31, 2022. Audible's help center says Microsoft discontinued the Amazon Appstore on Windows 11 and that the Audible Android app "is no longer available or supported on Windows 11".

Audible's Conditions of Use, in the versions dated September 10, 2025 and November 2, 2026, say "When you purchase content from Audible, you are purchasing a license", subject to the rights and restrictions of Audible's License. The License, dated February 18, 2025, grants buyers who comply with it and the other Terms, including payment of any applicable fees, a "limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, non-sublicensable license" for "personal and non-commercial use of the purchased content". A note in Audible's help on removing titles from the Library says "The titles you purchase with a credit or credit card are yours to keep".

The Conditions of Use dated March 31, 2022 and September 10, 2025 encouraged buyers "to download the content promptly after purchase". Both said Audible "may continue" to make purchased content available for re-download but did "not guarantee" it. The version dated November 2, 2026 no longer contains those sentences. The 2022, 2025 and 2026 versions all forbid any attempt to "disable, bypass, modify, defeat, or otherwise circumvent" digital rights management (DRM) or any other protection system applied to Audible content.

Lifehacker writer Emily Long wrote on September 16, 2026 that people who buy titles on Audible would "expect that the files are yours to keep", but that "this isn't a guarantee". Consumer advocate Louis Rossmann said in a March 2024 video that he would no longer pay for audiobooks unless he got a file, such as an Opus or Vorbis file, that he could play on his own device.

The technology news site The Verge reported that, starting February 26, 2025, Amazon was removing a website feature that let buyers download purchased books to a computer and then copy them manually to a Kindle e-reader over USB. A pop-up warning on Amazon's website, reproduced by The Verge, said that from that date "the 'Download & Transfer via USB' option will no longer be available". Amazon spokesperson Jackie Burke said in a statement to The Verge that customers could continue reading books previously downloaded on their Kindle device and access new content through the Kindle app, Kindle for web and Kindle devices with WiFi capability.

The technology site Android Authority reported in December 2025 that, starting January 20, 2026, buyers of a qualifying DRM-free title would be able to download an EPUB (an e-book format that can be used on devices other than a Kindle) or PDF version, while most Kindle books would still not be downloadable.

In a February 2025 video, Rossmann argued that removing the download button helped nobody but maybe rights holders and Amazon, and did not help the end user.

Good e-Reader wrote that for users who want to download their entire library to a PC or Mac "for safe-keeping", the community relies on "dedicated tools that bypass the missing web buttons".

  • Libation describes itself as "a free, open-source application for downloading and managing your Audible audiobooks".
  • The audible-cli project calls itself "A powerful command-line tool for managing and downloading your Audible audiobooks", a program run through commands such as "audible library list".
  • OpenAudible's website says the program connects to an Audible account, downloads the entire library and converts it to MP3 or M4B audio files; it is "Free to try", but "Conversion and splitting require a license", a paid OpenAudible license sold as "one payment, no subscription".

OpenAudible's documentation says that when a user signs in, the program "registers a virtual device with Amazon", and that version 5.0.3 or later "registers new sign-ins as an Android device". Libation's developer wrote on the project's issue tracker in September 2026 that Libation "tries hard to essentially mimic the official app". OpenAudible's documentation says Audible "recently changed which registrations it accepts" and refuses download licenses to "some registrations made by OpenAudible 5.0.2 and earlier". Libation's release notes said that when Audible refuses a license because an account is being throttled, users should "Wait 24 to 48 hours", as it is "Audible rate-limiting, not a Libation bug"; a later release fixed "widespread 'License Denied' / CustomerThrottled failures" caused by Libation registering Android devices with a serial number twice the expected length.

In a September 2025 video, Rossmann said he had used programs that let buyers get audio files of their Audible books, without guilt because he had paid for the books. He said he thought the program was called Open Audible, a Linux program he had downloaded a few years earlier, but that he could be wrong.

items.title: Diablo II
items.author: doppp
items.content:
The aggressively Satanic imagery of the series — “Diablo” means “Devil” in Spanish — would have contributed to a moral panic ten or fifteen years earlier. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, everybody just went on with their day.

[Diablo II] is a progression with a character where you go and defeat enemies and get rewarded. There’s overriding goals as well as lots of sub-goals. There’s many things to do, yet it’s very simple. It’s very straightforward. There’s no, “What am I supposed to do now?” It’s pretty much in your face as to what you’re supposed to be doing. It’s very easy to click, and it does things automatically…

There’s never enough blood and fire.

Within a few weeks of the release of , it was clear that Blizzard Entertainment had a hit on their hands. Within a few months, it was clear that this was more than a hit: that it was another era-defining game from the company that had given the world only a year and a half earlier. Not to make a sequel once that realization had dawned would have been to leave a dump truck full of money parked on the curb.

Fortunately, it wasn’t hard for Blizzard’s upper management to convince David Brevik, Max and Erich Schaefer, and the rest of their team at Blizzard North to throw themselves into such a project. They saw as a chance to implement all of the things they hadn’t had the time or resources for back when the first game was an unproven shot in the dark, as well as to fix the infelicities that had cropped up once players had gotten their hands on it in the wild. In their minds, this was to be as much as it was .

Yet they knew that they had to tread carefully as they made their improvements, lest they lose the qualities that had made the first game so popular. had homed in relentlessly on a simple gameplay loop of (minimal) effort and (maximal) reward: go into dungeons, kill monsters, collect loot, and level up. Rinse and repeat, until you reached the sixteenth dungeon level out of sixteen, beat the last boss, and won the game. Story and setting, strategic and tactical nuance, and all of the other complexities that normally went into the CRPG genre were curtailed or eliminated entirely in homage to the loop, Brevik having intuited — correctly, as the sales figures showed — that a lot of gamers didn’t actually care about that stuff. A sequel which reintroduced too many of the very elaborations that had pared away risked no longer feeling like  at all, a danger of which the team was well aware.

Thus the three years it took them to make were filled with a lot of hand-wringing and second-guessing about how much additional complexity was too much. “In hindsight it feels like it was all fine, we got to where we got, why were we ever worried about it?” says character artist and dialog writer Phil Shenk. “But in the middle of it, yeah, there were times that we felt like we were messing with the formula or that we were ruining it.” They learned to evaluate every mooted change through the lens of a single mission statement: “We aren’t making a CRPG. We’re making a .”

Shenk was one of about 40 people who joined Brevik and his 20 or so colleagues who had helped to create . Despite the tripling of manpower, it took them far, far longer than anticipated to finish the sequel. Those three years were a period of rapid change in the games industry, marked by consolidation in terms of both publishers and gameplay formulas. It is a measure of Blizzard’s enormous success and influence that two of the three most popular such formulas could be traced back to that company: there was a flood of real-time-strategy titles seeking to duplicate the sales figures of , and a flood of so-called “action RPGs” trying to do the same for . As the turn of the millennium approached, the industry as a whole was increasingly the one that Blizzard and id Software — the inventor of the first-person shooter, the third hugely popular gameplay formula — had made in their image. The new heart of the market was fast-paced, violent, action-oriented in every sense of the phrase, and readily amenable to the online multiplayer matches that were becoming more and more of a priority for hardcore gamers as the state of Internet connectivity steadily improved.

Yet even Blizzard wasn’t entirely insulated from the more worrisome aspects of change and consolidation. Rather oddly in light of the company’s outsized influence as the most successful single studio and publisher of the age, Blizzard was not an independent entity. From 1994 until 1996, it had been owned by Davidson and Associates, a staid specialist in educational software. In June of 1996, it had been acquired along with its parent company by CUC, a strange and voracious shopping-club empire reigned over by a snazzily attired gentleman named Walter Forbes. Along with Blizzard, CUC had also picked up the venerable Sierra On-Line, thus capturing a prodigious chunk of where gaming was going and where it had been in one fell scoop. In December of 1997, CUC merged with an administrator of hotel, rental-car, and real-estate franchises called HFS to form a new conglomerate called Cendant Corporation. Just a few months later, the wheels came off.

Much of Blizzard North was on a junket to Las Vegas when the news broke in April of 1998 that something was rotten in the state of Cendant. “We’re in this hotel room, and all these panicked calls start coming in,” says David Brevik. “We turn on the news, and the number-one story is the Cendant scam. It was ridiculous. We were just watching the stock drop. It was painful.” It turned out that Walter Forbes had had a better knack for accounting fraud than he had for running shopping clubs.

The collapse of Cendant became the biggest American business scandal of the decade, with Blizzard, Sierra, and the rest of the conglomerate’s thoroughly misplaced games division dragged through the mud as unwilling hostages. Ironically, the scandal broke at virtually the same instant that , Blizzard’s next mega-hit, was shipping from the publisher’s more southerly offices.

For Sierra, a traditional specialist in adventure games whose products had fallen badly out of favor, the stakes were existential, and in the long run extinctionary. For Blizzard, the hot new whizz kids of the industry, they would prove less serious, for all that you might have had difficulty explaining that to the many Blizzard employees who had dutifully invested a portion of their paychecks into now-worthless Cendant stock. On November 20, 1998, the entirety of the spiraling Cendant games division was picked up by the French conglomerate Vivendi. Everyone understood that Blizzard was the real prize, the once-mighty Sierra merely the baggage that went along with the deal. And indeed, Sierra’s operations would soon be shuttered, the name allowed to live on as a brand only — and soon enough not even that. Blizzard, however, was permitted to continue with business as usual. For even the officious executives at Vivendi knew better than to kill the goose that just kept on laying golden eggs. Not only was well on its way to becoming Blizzard’s best-selling game yet, but  and  continued to sell better every single month than the vast majority of brand-new titles from other publishers, their appeal extended indefinitely by Blizzard’s pioneering Battle.net online matchmaking service, which meant that a quick pickup game with a real human was never more than a few mouse clicks away.

Over and above even Battle.net, the not-so-secret recipe for Blizzard’s commercial winning streak was the combination of a laser-sharp attunement to the desires and priorities of the typical young male gamer with an uncompromising commitment to execution and polish in service to those priorities. Blizzard’s staff, both in the North and the South, understood their customers so well because they their customers, even as they worked so hard to make their games as good as they could possibly be for the same reason. Business itself was a kind of grand multiplayer game to them; the last thing they wanted to do was release a bad and/or poor-selling product that would spoil their winning streak. Thus their willingness to tear everything up and go back to the drawing board on a project, as they did early in the development of , or to abandon entirely projects that had begun to seem out of tune with the gamer zeitgeist, as they did a adventure game when it became clear that that dog just wasn’t hunting anymore. (Witness: the fate of their Cendant stablemate Sierra.)

Still, the wiggle room that the ongoing success of gave Blizzard North as they worked on the sequel only extended so far. The last eighteen months of its development — fully half of the project’s total duration — was one brutal, endless crunch that became a bit much even for these hardcore souls. “It was, to this day, the worst crunch I’ve ever experienced on any project,” says programmer and sound designer Jonathan Stone. “It’s not something you want to keep doing into your thirties.” “You just don’t tell people to work twelve hours a day. It’s really taxing,” says programmer Peter Kemmer. “It drove me out of the company, and I’m sure it drove other people out, because there’s only so much of that you can take.”

The relatively small minority of the Blizzard staff who were married or in serious romantic relationships suffered particularly. Several divorces and breakups resulted from the crunch; among these casualties was David Brevik’s marriage. An older and wiser version of s primary mastermind is now all too aware of what his brainchild cost him as well as what it gave him, especially when it came to his relationship with his two daughters: “It scarred me for a long time. It had huge ramifications on my life, most of them pretty negative. It was extremely costly.” Even Max Schaefer, who as a member of the Blizzard North management team was one of the primary drivers of the crunch, has come to recognize that he may not have done his employees’ physical and mental health any favors: “Six months into this crunch period, you’re still going, and you’re not really close to being done, although it always seemed like you were two or three months out. You start to physically and mentally burn out.”

In such circumstances, the colleagues with whom you were spending upwards of 80 hours per week became the sum total of your social life. “Everyone I knew at Blizzard became my circle,” says tester Josh Kurtz. “It became my support structure, my family. I did everything with them.” It was the ultimate recipe for instilling the very same hardcore monoculture, all but impenetrable to outsiders, that Blizzard was making such hay out of serving. Although David Brevik had famously told the team who worked on that it should be straightforward enough for their moms to pick up and play, it’s safe to say that not too many mothers were playing Blizzard games out there in the real world. Meanwhile the crunch cycles that made a job in the games industry incompatible with a balanced family and social life did indeed serve to drive most people out of it by the time they reached the end of their twenties, further reinforcing the sense of stultifying sameness that so marked the values and aesthetics of computer gaming during this period. The so-called “casual revolution” of the aughts was partially a response to the “gamerdark” vibe of outfits like Blizzard, offering up a vision of gaming that was at least markedly different, if not always more broadminded, in its own values and aesthetics.

In the here and now of Y2K, however, the hardcore monoculture was capable of generating outsized amounts of money if you hit it just right, as Blizzard had a better aptitude for doing than anyone else. By the time was finally pronounced done in June of 2000, its predecessor had sold a cool 2.5 million units and was still prominent on the shelves of every games store in the country, despite its age of three and a half years — donkey’s years in gaming terms. Other action RPGs like , , and — everyone seemed to be searching for punchy one-word titles like — had shifted their fair share of units as well, although none had come close to matching their primary inspiration’s numbers. Blizzard was so confident in the sequel’s prospects that they shelled out for an initial production run of 2 million copies before they ever shipped the first box to a store.

That decision proved not to have been overconfident. Far from it. didn’t just perpetuate Blizzard’s winning streak; it amplified it. That 2-million-copy run sold through in just six weeks; 184,000 copies were sold in the first 24 hours alone, leading the Guinness Book of World Records to crown the fastest-selling computer game of all time. (This record would eventually be broken by — wouldn’t you know it? — another Blizzard game.)

One of the few areas where did depart from the established code of hardcore gaming was ironically one of the keys to its sales. In a milieu where young men competed with one another to put together the hottest gaming “rig” in much the same way that their fathers might have competed to own the fastest car, Blizzard kept the system requirements of their games counterintuitively modest. ran at a fixed screen resolution of just 640 X 480, the same as its predecessor, and used a fancy 3D graphics card as an optional visual enhancer rather than a baseline requirement. It could run acceptably well on a 233 MHz Pentium I with just 32 MB of memory, specs which some widely available laptops exceeded with ease by the year of its release. If you wanted to feel up with the times in gaming but you couldn’t afford to buy or build an expensive wundermachine, was the answer to your prayers. You could jump on Battle.net and make a name for yourself without anyone having to know you were borrowing your mom’s work computer. Suffice to say that there are always great rewards to be reaped in casting as wide a net as possible — even if “dated” graphics did become one of the few points that s reviewers could find to grumble about in their otherwise glowing testimonials.

Such complaints were sour drops in a tidal wave. became the rare computer game capable of withstanding commercial comparisons with older, more widely adopted forms of media; for a while there, it was outselling , the much-anticipated fourth book in the Harry Potter series. It would still be capable of sneaking onto top-ten games charts as late as 2010, even as Battle.net would swarm with more players at that late date than it ever had before. The game’s lifetime sales, which are still being added to in a significant way to this day via digital storefronts, must surely number well into the tens of millions, dwarfing even the enormous success of by an order of magnitude and a whole lot more.

s four acts are separated by the most elaborate and extended cutscenes Blizzard had created to this point. They may have little to do with the rest of the game, but they’re certainly impressive to watch, easily the most visually impressive part of the whole experience.

Of course, low system requirements were far from the only reason for s mind-boggling success. Blizzard North really did find ways of making the notoriously addictive even more so, whilst making sure that their game continued to feel every inch a . They figured out where they could build on what had come before and where they had best leave well enough alone.

The first game had sprung a deliciously twisted surprise ending on you, by promoting the character you had been playing all along to the position of the inheritor of the throne of the evil demon Diablo, the Big Bad he had just vanquished. This means that when you, as a veteran, create another character to do battle against the Big Bad in , you’re going to war in a sense against your own former self. This series is hardly noted for its thematic ambitions, but props where they are due for the Freudian audacity of this conceit.

Much more important to the large majority of players then and now, however, is the nature of the environments and the gameplay that you find yourself cast into. And here the most obvious change is that is  than what came before — much, much bigger. The game is divided into four acts, the first three of which are each easily as large as the original . Only the climax, which takes place in Hell itself, is a little shorter, both because the developers were running out of time and energy by that point and because a more abbreviated endgame just felt right to them in terms of pacing. Each act revolves around a home base much like the afflicted town of Tristram in , a safe space to which to return to buy and sell items and treasure and heal up for the next expedition into danger.

But while the basic gameplay rhythm within each act is the same as that of , there’s another massive difference in the details. Instead of exploring a linear series of randomly-generated dungeon levels that open up one by one as you progress, in the mold of the roguelike games that were s first and most important influence, here you get to wander the countryside in search of less linear adventure, guided only by a series of broad quests which you are given to fulfill and the waypoints that are placed on the map to guide you to and through them. The terrain encompasses everything from swamps to deserts, forests to mountains, culminating in the aforementioned infernal realms. Most of it too is randomly generated, with only occasional pre-crafted set-pieces, usually marking the conclusions of the quests. You’ll still spend plenty of time underground before all is said and done, in the various caves and dungeons you find scattered about the landscapes, but the open-world design does as much as the sheer added length to make the sequel feel epic in comparison to the first game. This does not uniformly delight everyone; there is an argument to be made that is actually the purer, tighter game design of the two. But the reality is that relatively few gamers in 2000 or at any point afterward were going to complain about trading a 12-hour game for a 40-hour one.

Unlike , which presented you with a randomized subset of a list of possible quests on each play-through, the quests in are always the same. There are six of them in the first three acts, three in the last one. Like everything else about the game, they’re kept simple and straightforward.

Almost as impactful is the new approach to character-building. David Brevik understood well how intrinsic the bond between player and avatar is to the appeal of games like this one. In fact, he felt that didn’t go as far as it ought to have in that area. In that game, you could choose from one of three archetypal character classes, the Warrior, the Rogue, and the Sorcerer. Each had its distinct area of strength — for the Warrior it was melee combat, for the Rogue it was ranged combat, for the Sorcerer it was magic — but all could to some extent cross the borders of their archetypes to acquire talents associated with the other classes. As a result, characters tended to grow less rather than more unique as the game went on. What was the point in having classes at all if each one was destined to end up in roughly the same place, wondered Brevik and his team as they embarked upon the sequel. In this do-over, they were determined to make sure that the player, having chosen a class at the beginning of , would still be reckoning with the consequences of that choice 40 hours later at the climax.

Their first change to the class system was in keeping with many of the other changes they made to the sequel: to give you classes to choose from, five instead of three, known this time as the Necromancer, the Amazon, the Paladin, the Sorceress, and the Barbarian. But that alone would do nothing to solve the problem of the classes blurring together over time. To address that issue, Brevik found inspiration in an unlikely source: the classic 4X grand-strategy game .

In that game and many others of its ilk, you need to increase your civilization’s level of technology via research, trade, or espionage, so that you can build faster and more fearsome spaceships, colonize inhospitable planets which you otherwise couldn’t, etc. But is ingeniously designed to make it practically impossible to acquire of the technologies on the tech tree (or at least not before the question has become moot). Choice and happenstance dictate that you will be forced to work with a different mix of technological strengths and weaknesses every time you start a new game, forced to adapt your strategy appropriately; this is one of the keys to s uncanny longevity, one of the reasons it is considered such a classic.

Brevik imported a system much like that one into s character building. As your character levels up, he receives points which you can invest into skills — 150 skills in all, 30 for each character class, with absolutely no crossover from class to class. This alone serves to ensure that each class stays unique from first to last. But then goes much further than this, in order to ensure that not just each character class but each remains unique. In the course of a typical play-through, you can expect to earn about 35 skill points. This is nowhere near enough to cover all of the 30 skills your character can theoretically learn, meaning that you have to choose areas of specialization a class. Thus one person’s Necromancer is all but guaranteed to play very differently from another’s. Maybe the one concentrates on building golems from mud and clay, while the other prefers to raise up hordes of skeletons from the corpses of enemies. The same principle applies to all of the other classes.

The Paladin’s skill tree. Skills are grouped into three broad categories. Within each category, they become more expensive as you move from left to right. So, another choice that confronts you is whether to buy a wide variety of less powerful skills or to save up your points for one or two really devastating ones.

As a matter of personal preference, I’m lukewarm at best on , but I don’t hesitate to admit that this character-building system is absolutely brilliant. In my opinion, it’s the best, most innovative single design choice that was made for the game. Needless to say, it lends enormous replayability for those who are buying the core experience which  is selling. To further encourage you to start all over again as soon as you finish the game the first time, an advanced difficulty level, known as Nightmare, opens up for characters who have triumphed at the standard difficulty. And then an even more advanced one, known as simply Hell, opens once they’ve finished on Nightmare. Blizzard did not build their games in the expectation that they would be played through once and then set aside.

The definitive expression of that ideology was the online multiplayer modes that had been included in every Blizzard game since , and greatly enhanced since the release of by the Battle.net service. Despite its pioneering status, multiplayer had actually been something of a last-minute addition to the first , implemented by a team that was helicoptered in from Blizzard South while Blizzard North was trying to get the rest of the game finished. The end results displayed that in some unfortunate ways. All of the data pertaining to one’s character was stored locally on one’s own computer — an open invitation to break out the old hex editor and start cheating. And this players most definitely did, until online had become a preposterous circus of tricksters, grifters, and griefers.

Blizzard fixed most of those problems for , by the simple expedient of storing Battle.net characters on their own servers instead of on their players’ hard drives. Knowing well how important online play had been to the stunning uptake of , Blizzard was a good, careful steward of this aspect of . Up to eight players could roam simultaneously through the landscapes from any of the game’s four acts, where they could choose to join together to defeat the monsters, engage in free-for-all battle with one another, or divide up into teams to do a little of both. Like single-player , it wasn’t the deepest experience to be had in the world of gaming, but plenty of people found it plenty compelling, especially at Battle.net’s asking price of completely free to anyone who had gone out and bought the game. (Blizzard was able to offer this free service largely because the game sessions themselves still employed a client-to-client architecture once the characters being played had been downloaded from the official servers; this kept bandwidth costs to a minimum.) Blizzard encouraged guilds and other forms of socializing to keep people coming back and ran leader boards and the like to keep the competitive fires burning, all of it for literal decades after first hit stores. Throughout the aughts and beyond, hundreds of thousands of players could regularly be found on Battle.net enjoying their host’s largesse.

isn’t the sort of game that looks all that nice in screenshots. In practice, however, its special effects convey palpably your character’s increasing powers as you climb the skill tree.

So, for a certain kind of commercially focused games studio — exactly the kind that Blizzard happened to be — was the veritable Platonic ideal of a sequel. It fixed its predecessor’s few flaws whilst being dramatically bigger, plus deeper in the handful of places where it could get away with it without losing its fundamental -ness. And somehow Blizzard North managed to make the interface through which all of this happened even more elegantly intuitive than before; this was the element that the many people who made “ clones” never could quite figure out how to match. Small wonder that sold like $1 ice-cream cones on the hottest day of the year.

As for me: my own reservations about echo those I already expressed in my article on . Even with the modicum of extra depth that the revamped class system in particular lends to the sequel, it’s still a game where you spend most of your time roaming over algorithmically generated terrain and clicking on monsters fairly mindlessly until they die. The folks at Blizzard North made no secret that they were consciously trying to make their game as addictive as crack cocaine, by appealing directly to the lizard brain’s pleasure centers: kill ever bigger monsters, find ever better stuff, grow ever stronger, all without having to expend too much mental energy on the endeavor. Blizzard programmer Peter Kemmer describes as “basically slot machines inside of slot machines inside of slot machines,” a meticulously engineered dopamine-delivery system. For me, is gaming’s equivalent of junk food: it feels really good to eat at first, then becomes hard to stop eating, even after it has begun to feel less good. Much though I have to admire and  alike for their real achievements in design and implementation, I do prefer to play games that don’t feel quite so calculating, ones that are able to engage me in the more — for lack of a better word — ways that they never even attempt.

But then again, as I’ve said a million times before: I’m just one guy on the Internet. You do you, my friends. Even the most health-conscious of us sometimes just wants to open a big bag of chips and go to town.

Another addition to was mercenaries who could be hired to help you with tough fights. The expansion pack made it possible for them to accompany you through the whole game, gaining levels just like your main character. This effectively turned into a party-based game, if you chose to play it that way. (And note also what a distinct difference the expansion pack’s resolution bump makes…)

Blizzard’s crowning achievement in the context of came precisely one year after it was first released, when they shipped the expansion pack. Unlike , the disowned stepchild of an expansion to , this pack was developed in-house by the same people who had made the base game to which it was attached. They added another slate of fit-and-finish improvements to an already ridiculously polished game, including an optional bump in the graphics resolution to 800 X 600. (Cue the sarcastic comments from hardcore gamers to whom this was still a stone-age figure.) There were also two new character classes with new skill trees, while the heart of the matter was a fifth act to play through once the first four had been finished. sold predictably well, until it was integrated into the that would remain a fixture on store shelves until the very idea of buying computer games on physical media began to seem anachronistic.

wouldn’t arrive until 2012. Partly this was down to the departure of a burnt-out David Brevik from Blizzard, partly to the distraction of running , the most popular MMORPG of all time. (In other words, Blizzard’s winning streak continued.) But I suspect that the biggest stumbling block may have been that it just wasn’t clear where to with a third . The second game had mastered the brief to such a degree of refined perfection that the prospects for further improvements seemed only marginal. That did still leave the possibility of doing something daringly different — except that the brand had become so closely identified with a specific gameplay model that the reception of any such departure would be doubtful in the extreme, even if Blizzard had been the type of studio to indulge in such conceptual leaps. So, all that was left was to wait for enough time to pass and for computing technology to improve enough that the old formula could seem fresh again inside a new suit of audiovisual clothing. After a couple of false starts, this is exactly what Blizzard wound up doing.

Even today, when not only a third but a fourth game have joined it in the series, remains a monument in its own right. Earlier in the very year that I find myself writing these words, Blizzard released a remastered version of the game, creating in the process new bosses to fight, a quarter-century after the last new content. It shot up the bestseller charts all over again, winning fans who hadn’t yet been born when was fresh on store shelves. Clearly its algorithmic, friction-free approach holds up for many people today as well as ever. Yes, it does leave me with mixed feelings in some ways — and yet I would be the last person to deny that knows what it wants to do and pulls it off with stupendous aplomb. The slot machines continue to whir as enticingly as ever.

items.title: Knuth: Moratorium on Error Reports
items.author: ultraficial
items.content:
For more than fifty years I've been welcoming reports from readers of errors in my books, so that I can correct them before new copies are printed.

Alas, the rise of LLMs has increased the productivity of my readers so greatly that error reports are now being submitted much faster than I can read them!

This content is very important to me, and I wish to take personal responsibility for getting everything right. Therefore I insist on verifying everything carefully.

That takes time. But the amount of available time is now less than zero.

Random sampling indicates that the vast majority of errors that have been reported in recent weeks are repeats of issues already submitted by others.

Therefore, I shall not be able to look at any error reports submitted after 25 November, 2026, until I've posted an updated list of the known errors in whatever book is involved.

Please consult the list below to see if error reports are currently being accepted.

I apologize for having made errors in the first place, and for having limited ability to cope with more than one thing at a time. I shall do my best to get through the existing reports as soon as humanly possible.

Thanks in advance for your patience and understanding.

  • (At the moment I'm swamped, but hoping to add items to this list soon.]

items.title: Google's DeepCrossAttention achieves comparable model quality up to 3x faster
items.author: ComputedCamp995
items.content:
Think of a traditional deep learning model like a giant game of "Telephone": data passes through layer after layer, with each layer changing the information slightly. If a network has dozens or hundreds of layers, the original learning signal can become severely degraded or lost by the time it reaches all layers, which is known as the vanishing gradient problem in AI.

To overcome this challenge and enable the training of networks with dozens or hundreds of layers, transformers rely heavily on residual connections, also known as “skip” connections, which act like an information highway or a shortcut. Instead of forcing the data to pass exclusively through the complicated layer, a duplicate copy of the original input skips right past this layer and is added directly to its output. This ensures that the model always has the original raw data to refer back to.

The standard residual connection implements a simple operation: point-wise summation of a layer's output with its input. While computationally efficient, this simple process has a key limitation: it treats all prior representations with equal weight, leading to information dilution in deep networks. As features propagate through many layers, specific, high-resolution details from earlier layers can be averaged out or distorted, making it difficult for the network to selectively retrieve them. This forces the network to recompute them, reducing learning efficiency.

In our ICML 2025 paper, "DeepCrossAttention: Supercharging Transformer Residual Connections," we studied the shortcomings of the traditional residual architecture and introduced DeepCrossAttention (DCA), which generalizes residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from the history of preceding layers. By allowing the model to dynamically choose which previous layers are most important at any given moment, DCA achieves comparable or improved learning, while reducing the number of parameters needed by up to 30-40%.

items.title: Credit card skimming scripts using WebRTC found on popular shopping sites
items.author: scanr
items.content:
Which sites were affected

On November 24, we notified all of the named parties in this article and others, including: Amazon Web Services about the storage buckets serving the script, Cloudflare about the services the malefactor used, the domain registrars, the pixel vendor, the consent-banner provider and the affected retailers and platforms. Lascana replied to us and removed the Quorum pixel from their site by November 24th at 15:48 UTC. Quorum confirmed the identified malicious code was removed from their pixel tracker, and they restored the clean marketing pixel as of November 24th at 21:09 UTC.

Revolve provided this statement on behalf of REVOLVE and FWRD: “On November 25, InfoHawk notified our team of a potential security issue impacting mobile and tablet versions of our websites which we resolved the same day. We appreciate the outreach, and are actively investigating the issue to determine any potential impact.”

Quorum is an ad-attribution platform that links ad views to store visits and online sales (quorum.inc).

Seers is a cookie consent management platform and data privacy compliance company (seers.ai).

This attack uses WebRTC, the technology that allows you to make video calls in your web browser. WebRTC lets a web page open its own channel to another party and pass data (e.g. audio/video packets) over it. It has likely been used (both to load the skimmer and to send the stolen card details out) because security rules and monitoring tools often do not watch this communications channel as closely. For example, Meta briefly used WebRTC in a creative way in 2025, according to researchers looking at the technology as a compromise vector. This form of attack appears to target mobile devices, and we only saw the server enable the skimmer on checkout pages, so desktop checks and homepage scans would likely not see it. The skimmer's traffic appeared to run through Cloudflare's relay, so it would blend in with the WebRTC traffic and hide its true endpoint.

The skimmer and card details both traveled over WebRTC

How the kit is designed to work on a store page, in 7 steps. Only step 4 is an ordinary web request, which a rule can block; steps 5 to 7 run over the WebRTC data channel, outside .

  1. The loader gets onto the page through a consent-banner setting, a retailer CDN file, a shared marketing pixel or the store's own HTML.

  2. Loading scripts from S3 buckets

    It loads or from an Amazon S3 bucket.

  3. Targeting the attack to mobile checkouts

    It runs only on small or touch screens. The Samsonite version runs on only.

  4. Establishing the WebRTC connection

    fetches the relay details, and sends the WebRTC offer, to a brand-named host.

  5. Data exchange via TURN relay

    Every exchange that returned relay details used . The malefactor's answers listed only Cloudflare relay addresses; through that relay it sends code and receives data.

  6. Attack code is loaded and executed

    The skimmer arrives in chunks over the channel, is checked against a SHA-256 digest, then run with .

  7. Data goes back the same way

    At Lascana's checkout, the skimmer sent our test card details this way.

This was the only example of live card details being sent off-site that we captured.

Worried that your card was compromised?

Check your recent statements for charges you don't recognize, especially on debit cards. Call your bank or card issuer right away, report the fraud and ask for a new card number. Follow up with a written dispute within 60 days of the statement that shows the charge.

Our understanding of US federal law is that your liability for unauthorized credit card charges is capped at $50, and is generally zero if only your card number was stolen, as in a skimming attack like this one. Debit cards have weaker protections that depend on how quickly you report, so act fast. For more information, see “Additional resources” below.

What site owners should immediately do

On every page that takes payment, set a rule that lists only the hosts you use.

That blocks the two web requests the script needs before WebRTC opens. Without them the skimmer never arrives, whichever file was tampered with.

What security teams should look for

We saw the skimmer delivered in three different ways across five websites run by different companies, and all of them appear to rely on the same attacker infrastructure. That makes it likely that other sites are affected too, so we encourage online retailers to check their own sites for the signs below.

  1. search page source, tag managers, consent-banner settings and CDN files for scripts from <brand>-static.s3.amazonaws[.]com (files , ). We believe this is the malicious code.
  2. if you load qscripts.s3.amazonaws[.]com/pscript.js, check its last line for one of the above CDN buckets, and if present, remove the tracking pixel. We recommend reviewing all similar tracking pixels and their exposure to sensitive fields or actions on your website.
  3. If you have integrated Seers, open your banner config (cdn.seersco.com/banners/<account>/<domain>/cb.js) and check that every URL field holds only a URL. In the affected configs, the privacy-policy link field also held a hidden image, whose event handler loaded the malicious code.
  4. on a phone-sized touch screen, at the payment step, look for and requests to and a relay-only WebRTC connection used by the malicious code. Desktop checks miss it.
  5. , and are referenced in the malicious code and may warrant further investigation if present.

The industry is not ready for the scale of supply chain attacks coming

This attack takes advantage of a few critical design decisions in websites that, if improperly configured, allow malicious actors to broadly deploy and trigger exploits across the open web.

  • Websites load third-party code, often through a tag manager, from servers they don't control. The vendor can change that code at any time, and it can pull in further third-party code the site never reviewed.
  • That code runs as an ordinary script with the same rights as the site's own code. It can read and rewrite the page, watch what users type, and load more code.
  • Login, personal-information and payment pages often load the same marketing scripts as the rest of the site. Card fields should sit in an isolated payment frame, and third-party tags should be kept off these pages entirely.

Loading third-party tracking pixels on checkout, payment and login pages is far too common a practice today. Each pixel can run whatever code its vendor's file holds, including a skimmer, and whoever controls that file can change it without the site noticing. Every site should review which tracking pixels load on pages that take payment or sign-in details, who can change those files, and whether they need to be there at all.

A similar weakness was exploited at scale on 16 November 2026. An attacker reportedly used a flaw in Optimizely's Web Experimentation product to add malicious code to customers' projects, and Optimizely's own servers delivered it to visitors of 178 organizations' sites, including Zoom, the BBC and CNN, with no change to those sites' own code.

items.title: Paolo Soleri built a utopian eco-city in the Arizona desert
items.author: robtherobber
items.content:
‘Arcosanti is traditionally about minimal living – a deliberate poverty of living simply for the sake of equity,’ says Ray Paskus, a resident of two years and an archivist for the Cosanti Foundation. Perhaps this is why so many co-living projects fail to last the journey. Arcosanti is the exception, not the rule – and it’s hardly thriving. Less than 10 per cent of Soleri’s masterplan has been realised and, despite a broader interest in communal living, Paskus says applications are at a standstill. ‘People project all sorts of things on to Arcosanti, but the lifestyle is harsh and isolating and full of hard work – it’s almost monastic. To grow the community you have to be able to sell that to people.’ There are few, he’s found, that are truly interested in the asceticism needed to make earth-conscious co-operative living work.

It’s a shame, he says, because a philosophy of reuse and collaborative living could be one solution to the ills of our time. Soleri died in 2013 at the age of 93, still convinced that ‘we must reinvent the city to develop our civilisation’. Arcosanti endures as that living sketch – unfinished, alive and quietly radical.

Edit: It is important to note that allegations of abuse have been made by Daniela Soleri about her father, the architect Paolo Soleri.

For more information, visit arcosanti.org. A version of this story appears in the March 2026 issue of ‘The World of Interiors’. Learn about our

items.title: Sydney Fire Ant Infestation
items.author: altilunium
items.content:
Authorities are ramping up efforts to manage a fire ant nest in Sydney after investigations revealed a larger and more complex infestation than first identified.

A nest detected in Auburn was successfully treated at the weekend, but further surveillance has revealed a more extensive presence of fire ants requiring intensive treatment and a broader biosecurity response.

It comes after Commonwealth authorities detected the insects, known for their painful sting, at the Enfield Intermodal Logistics Centre, in Sydney's inner west, on September 23.

Imported goods are suspected to be the source of both incursions, which are not otherwise believed to be connected.

NSW Agriculture Minister Tara Moriarty said a task force was being established to determine the ants' origins.

"The experts believe that they came in through containers that have come in likely from China," she said.

"At this stage, they are still only on this particular site in Auburn, but we will undertake further surveillance … to see if they have spread.

"I was able to check [the Auburn site] out myself yesterday, and even though the area is not geographically big, the types of ants that we have here do spread in a different way than what we've seen ants do in New South Wales."

Ms Moriarty said the Auburn infestation was located in an industrial area and included businesses that imported goods from Asia and elsewhere.

Management efforts underway

A biosecurity order is expected to be issued by Friday to regulate the movement of high-risk materials through Auburn, including soils, turf, mulch and building materials.

Additional biosecurity officers and detection dogs will also be deployed as part of the response.

Ms Moriarty said there had been more than 900 reports of suspicious nests from the public recent days, and asked locals to remain on the lookout for infestations.

"Biosecurity is everybody's responsibility,"

The ants are up to 6 millimetres long, dark reddish-brown with brown-black abdomens and are known to be aggressive.

Bites that have a burning sensation can cause itchy blisters or pustules and lead to the hospitalisation of children and death in severe cases.

If spotted, the nests must not be destroyed and members of the public are urged not to try to capture the ants, which are classified as prohibited matter in NSW.

Suspected fire ants can be reported to the Biosecurity Helpline on 1800 680 244.
